questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.17
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.questionHtml:
Zero has two representations in

  1. Sign-magnitude
  2. $2's$ complement
  3. $1's$ complement
  4. None of the above

review.concept: Digital Logic - Binary Signed Number Representations of Zero
review.notes: Sign-magnitude has +0 (00..0) and -0 (10..0). 1's complement has +0 (00..0) and -0 (11..1). 2's complement has a unique zero. Matches official key [A, C].

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2-18, ISRO2008-46
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.questionHtml:
Raid configurations of the disks are used to provide

  1. Fault-tolerance 

  2. High speed

  3. High data density

  4. (A) & (B)

review.concept: Operating Systems / Storage Architecture - RAID Capabilities and Objectives
review.notes: RAID provides fault tolerance (via mirroring/parity) and high speed (via disk striping). Matches official key D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.19
questions.subject: CO & Architecture
questions.questionHtml:
Arrange the following configuration for CPU in decreasing order of operating speeds:

Hard wired control, Vertical microprogramming, Horizontal microprogramming.

  1. Hard wired control, Vertical microprogramming, Horizontal microprogramming.

  2. Hard wired control, Horizontal microprogramming, Vertical microprogramming.

  3. Horizontal microprogramming, Vertical microprogramming, Hard wired control.

  4. Vertical microprogramming, Horizontal microprogramming, Hard wired control.

review.concept: Computer Organization & Architecture - Control Unit Implementation Speeds
review.notes: Speed ranking: Hardwired (gate delay) > Horizontal microprogrammed (ROM read, no decode) > Vertical microprogrammed (ROM read + decode delay). Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.21
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.questionHtml:
If $T_1 = O(1)$, give the correct matching for the following pairs:
$\begin{array}{l|l}\hline \text{(M) $T_n = T_{n-1} + n$} & \text{(U) $T_n = O(n)$} \\\hline \text{(N) $T_n = T_{n/2} + n$} & \text{(V) $T_n = O(n \log n)$} \\\hline \text{(O) $T_n = T_{n/2} + n \log n$} & \text{(W) $T_n = O(n^2)$} \\\hline \text{(P) $T_n = T_{n-1} + \log n$} & \text{(X) $T_n = O(\log^2 n)$} \\\hline \end{array}$

  1. $\text{M-W, N-V, O-U, P-X}$
  2. $\text{M-W, N-U, O-X, P-V}$
  3. $\text{M-V, N-W, O-X, P-U}$
  4. $\text{M-W, N-U, O-V, P-V}$

review.concept: Algorithms - Asymptotic Recurrence Relations and Master Theorem
review.notes: M: sum of 1..n is O(n^2) [W]; N: Master theorem gives O(n) [U]; O: geometric sum bounded by O(n log n) [V]; P: log(n!) is O(n log n) [V]. Matches official key D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.22
questions.subject: CO & Architecture
questions.questionHtml:
The main difference(s) between a CISC and a RISC processor is/are that a RISC processor typically

  1. has fewer instructions
  2. has fewer addressing modes
  3. has more registers
  4. is easier to implement using hard-wired logic

review.concept: Computer Organization & Architecture - RISC vs CISC Architecture Comparison
review.notes: RISC processors have fewer instructions (A), fewer addressing modes (B), larger register files (C), and simple hardwired control units (D). Matches official key [A, B, C, D].

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.23
questions.subject: CO & Architecture
questions.questionHtml:
A certain processor supports only the immediate and the direct addressing modes. Which of the following programming language features cannot be implemented on this processor?

  1. Pointers
  2. Arrays
  3. Records
  4. Recursive procedures with local variable

review.concept: Computer Organization & Architecture - Addressing Modes and Language Feature Implementation
review.notes: With only immediate and direct addressing, memory operands must have compile-time fixed addresses. Dynamic pointers, variable array indices, dynamic records, and recursive stack frames all require indirect/indexed/base addressing. Matches official key [A, B, C, D].

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.24
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following $C$ function definition

int Trial (int a, int b, int c)
{
    if ((a>=b) && (c<b)) return b;
    else if (a>=b) return Trial(a, c, b);
    else return Trial(b, a, c);
}

The functional Trial:

  1. Finds the maximum of $a$, $b$, and $c$

  2. Finds the minimum of $a$, $b$, and $c$

  3. Finds the middle number of $a$, $b$, $c$

  4. None of the above

review.concept: Algorithms / Programming in C - Function Tracing and Median Selection
review.notes: For b = c (e.g. Trial(5,3,3)), condition c < b fails and it recursively calls Trial(a, c, b) with identical arguments indefinitely. Thus it does not properly implement any option. Matches official key D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.25
questions.subject: Databases
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following is/are correct?

  1. An SQL query automatically eliminates duplicates
  2. An SQL query will not work if there are no indexes on the relations
  3. SQL permits attribute names to be repeated in the same relation
  4. None of the above

review.concept: Databases - SQL Relational Query Language Principles
review.notes: SQL preserves duplicates by default, functions via table scans without indexes, and requires unique column names within a relation. Matches official key D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.20
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.questionHtml:
The minimum number of record movements required to merge five files A (with $10$ records), B (with $20$ records), C (with $15$ records), D (with $5$ records) and E (with $25$ records) is:

  1. $165$
  2. $90$
  3. $75$
  4. $65$

review.concept: Algorithms - Optimal Merge Patterns and Greedy Record Movements
review.notes: Optimal 2-way merge greedy steps: (5+10)=15, (15+15)=30, (20+25)=45, (30+45)=75. Total movements = 15 + 30 + 45 + 75 = 165. Matches official key A.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 13
questions.subject: CO & Architecture
questions.questionHtml: An instruction pipeline consists of $4$ stages – Fetch $(F)$, Decode field $(D)$, Execute $(E)$ and Result Write $(W)$. The $5$ instructions in a certain instruction sequence need these stages for the different number of clock cycles as shown by the table below $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Instruction} & \textbf {F} &\textbf {D} & \textbf {E} &  \textbf{W } \\\hline \textbf{1}& 1 & 2  & 1 & 1 \\\hline \textbf{2} & 1 & 2 & 2  & 1\\\hline  \textbf{3}& 2 & 1  & 3 & 2 \\\hline \textbf{4} & 1 & 3 & 2  & 1 \\\hline \textbf{5} & 1 & 2 & 1  & 2 \\\hline \end{array}$$ Find the number of clock cycles needed to perform the $5$ instructions.

review.concept: Computer Organization & Architecture - Non-Uniform Pipeline Stage Scheduling
review.notes: Tracing stage contention with resource stalls: I1 finishes at 5, I2 at 8, I3 at 12, I4 at 13, and I5 finishes writeback at cycle 15. Matches official key 15.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 16
questions.subject: Other / Optional

review.concept: Compiler Design / Runtime Environments - Activation Records and Access Links
review.notes: Step-by-step runtime stack trace showing dynamic control links and static access links based on Pascal lexical nesting hierarchy.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 18
questions.subject: Other / Optional
questions.questionHtml:
Design a 2K $\times$ 8 (2048 locations, each 8 bit wide) memory system mapped at addresses (1000)$_{16}$ to (17FF)$_{16}$ for the 8085 processor using four 1K $\times$ 4 memory chips. Each of these chips has the following signal pins:

  1. $\overline{CS}$ (Chip select, data lines are in high impedance state when it is 1)

  2. $\overline{RD}$ (0 for read operation)

  3. $\overline{WR}$ (0 for write operation)

  4. $A_0, A_1, \dots A_9$ (input address lines. $A_0$ is the lest significant)

  5. $D_0, D_1, D_2, D_3$ (bi-directional data lines. $D_0$ is the least significant)

review.concept: Microprocessors / Hardware Design - 8085 Memory System Interfacing
review.notes: Complete memory interfacing design: 4 chips paired into two 1K x 8 banks, address decoding via 74LS138 for 1000H-17FFH, and full bus connections.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.3
questions.subject: Other / Optional
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following statements applies to the bisection method used for finding roots of functions:

  1. converges within a few iterations

  2. guaranteed to work for all continuous functions

  3. is faster than the Newton-Raphson method

  4. requires that there be no error in determining the sign of the function

review.concept: Engineering Mathematics - Numerical Methods and the Bisection Method
review.notes: The bisection method is guaranteed to converge for all continuous functions on a bracketing interval by the Intermediate Value Theorem. Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.9
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.questionHtml:
If the regular set $A$ is represented by $A = (01 + 1)^*$ and the regular set $B$ is represented by $B = \left(\left(01\right)^*1^*\right)^*$, which of the following is true?

  1. $A \subset B$
  2. $B \subset A$
  3. $A$ and $B$ are incomparable
  4. $A = B$

review.concept: Theory of Computation - Regular Expression Equivalence and Algebraic Identities
review.notes: By the fundamental regular expression algebraic identity (R* S*)* = (R + S)*, ((01)* 1*)* = (01 + 1)*, proving A = B. Matches official key D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.10
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following set can be recognized by a Deterministic Finite state Automaton?

  1. The numbers $1, 2, 4, 8, \dots 2^n, \dots$ written in binary

  2. The numbers $1, 2, 4, 8,\dots 2^n, \dots$  written in unary

  3. The set of binary string in which the number of zeros is the same as the number of ones.

  4. The set $\{1, 101, 11011, 1110111, \dots\}$

review.concept: Theory of Computation - Languages Recognizable by Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA)
review.notes: Powers of 2 in binary is the regular language 10*, which is recognized by a 2-state DFA. All other options require unbounded memory. Matches official key A.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.11
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.questionHtml:
Regarding the power of recognition of languages, which of the following statements is false?

  1. The non-deterministic finite-state automata are equivalent to deterministic finite-state automata.

  2. Non-deterministic Push-down automata are equivalent to deterministic Push-down automata.

  3. Non-deterministic Turing machines are equivalent to deterministic Turing machines.

  4. Multi-tape Turing machines are available are equivalent to Single-tape Turing machines.

review.concept: Theory of Computation - Computational Power of Deterministic vs Non-Deterministic Automata
review.notes: NPDAs recognize all CFLs while DPDAs recognize only DCFLs (DCFL is a strict proper subset of CFL). Hence NPDAs and DPDAs are not equivalent. Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.12
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.questionHtml:
The string $1101$ does not belong to the set represented by

  1. $110^*(0 + 1)$
  2. $1(0 + 1)^*101$
  3. $(10)^*(01)^*(00 + 11)^*$
  4. $(00 + (11)^*0)^*$

review.concept: Theory of Computation - String Membership in Regular Expressions
review.notes: 1101 is generated by A (11.0.1) and B (1.eps.101). It cannot be generated by C (ends in 01 which (00+11)* cannot produce) or D (every non-empty string in D ends in 0). Matches official key [C, D].

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.13
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.questionHtml:
What happens when a bit-string is XORed with itself $n$-times as shown:

$\left[B \oplus (B \oplus ( B \oplus (B \dots n \text{ times}\right]$

  1. complements when $n$ is even

  2. complements when $n$ is odd

  3. divides by $2^n$ always

  4. remains unchanged when $n$ is even

review.concept: Digital Logic - Boolean XOR Properties and Parity Invariants
review.notes: XORing B with itself n times: for n even, an odd number of B's are combined yielding B (remains unchanged); for n odd, pairs cancel to 0. Matches official key D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.14
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.questionHtml:
A multiplexer with a $4-bit$ data select input is a

  1. $4:1$ multiplexer
  2. $2:1$ multiplexer
  3. $16:1$ multiplexer
  4. $8:1$ multiplexer

review.concept: Digital Logic - Multiplexer Sizing and Select Line Relationships
review.notes: A multiplexer with k select lines has 2^k input lines. For k = 4, 2^4 = 16, giving a 16:1 multiplexer. Matches official key C.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.15
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.questionHtml:
The threshold level for logic 1 in the TTL family is

  1. any voltage above 2.5 V
  2. any voltage between 0.8 V and 5.0 V
  3. any voltage below 5.0 V
  4. any voltage below $V_{cc}$ but above 2.8 V

review.concept: Digital Logic - TTL Logic Level Voltage Thresholds
review.notes: TTL logic 1 level resides in the upper band below V_cc and above nominal high threshold (Option D). Matches official key D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.16
questions.subject: Unknown
questions.questionHtml:
In serial communication employing 8 data bits, a parity bit and 2 stop bits, the minimum band rate required to sustain a transfer rate of 300 characters per second is

  1. 2400 band
  2. 19200 band
  3. 4800 band
  4. 1200 band

review.concept: Computer Networks / Serial Communication - Baud Rate and Character Framing
review.notes: Frame size = 1 start + 8 data + 1 parity + 2 stop = 12 bits/char. 300 chars/s requires 300*12 = 3600 bps. Minimum standard baud rate to sustain 3600 is 4800 baud. Matches official key C.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.17
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.questionHtml:
The octal representation of an integer is $(342)_8$. If this were to be treated as an eight-bit integer in an $8085$ based computer, its decimal equivalent is

  1. $226$
  2. $-98$
  3. $76$
  4. $-30$

review.concept: Digital Logic / Microprocessors - Octal to Two's Complement Decimal Conversion
review.notes: Octal 342 in 8 bits is 11100010. In 2's complement, value is -128 + 64 + 32 + 2 = -30. Matches official key D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.18
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following devices should get higher priority in assigning interrupts?

  1. Hard disk
  2. Printer
  3. Keyboard
  4. Floppy disk

review.concept: Operating Systems / Computer Architecture - Interrupt Priority Assignment
review.notes: Hard disk has the highest data transfer rate and tightest latency constraints to prevent buffer overrun, requiring highest interrupt priority. Matches official key A.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.19
questions.subject: CO & Architecture
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following addressing modes permits relocation without any change whatsoever in the code?

  1. Indirect addressing

  2. Indexed addressing

  3. Base register addressing

  4. PC relative addressing

review.concept: Computer Organization & Architecture - Position-Independent Code and PC-Relative Addressing
review.notes: PC-relative addressing uses offsets relative to the PC, making branch displacements invariant under code relocation and enabling position-independent code (PIC). Matches official key D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.20
questions.subject: CO & Architecture
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following is true?

  1. Unless enabled, a CPU will not be able to process interrupts.

  2. Loop instructions cannot be interrupted till they complete.

  3. A processor checks for interrupts before executing a new instruction.

  4. Only level triggered interrupts are possible on microprocessors.

review.concept: Microprocessors / Operating Systems - Interrupt Handling and Processor Flags
review.notes: A CPU requires its interrupt enable flag to be set (e.g. via EI instruction) to service maskable interrupts. Interrupts are sampled at the end of instruction cycles. Matches official key A.
